courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.contribution: Mandatory Year-1 Personal & Professional Development.

evidenceFields.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.

courses.name: Introduction to Biodiversity
courses.contribution: Direct organismal diversity, phylogeny, identification and biodiversity measurement support marine-life and conservation inquiry; the survey spans terrestrial and aquatic life rather than reproducing a marine dissection/field sequence.

evidenceFields.description2: The biosphere consists of millions of living species. In this course we will travel through the tree of life, starting with bacteria and single-celled eukaryotes such as reef-building dinoflagellates and disease-causing apicomplexans. Next, we will look at the multicellular groups: plants, seaweeds, fungi and animals. We will also investigate the relevance of biodiversity for human society in fields such as food and food security, economy, climate and health.
evidenceFields.profile: Surveys the diversity and evolutionary relationships of living organisms across the tree of life. Students examine prokaryotes, protists, fungi, plants and animals, their distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement. A small project investigates a selected phylogenetic branch, supported by literature searching, data collection and analysis.
evidenceFields.topics: Biodiversity and its measurement; Phylogenetic relationships; Viruses; Bacteria and archaea; Protists; Fungi; Plant diversity; Invertebrates; Vertebrates and primates; Evolutionary history; Organismal ecological roles
evidenceFields.methods: Microscopy; Organism identification using identification apps; Rank-abundance diagrams; Species-saturation curves; Biodiversity indices; Phylogenetic research; Scholarly database searching; Biodiversity data collection and analysis

courses.name: Introduction to Economics
courses.contribution: Complementary supply/demand, incentives, strategic interaction, production and market allocation provide economic foundations for competing ocean uses; macroeconomic sections do not constitute marine-resource economics.

evidenceFields.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
evidenceFields.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
evidenceFields.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

courses.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
courses.contribution: Direct applied sustainability research with a Zeeland partner requires literature review, question/design, investigation and a final product. The project supplies research practice; its subject and methods depend on the partner, so marine field sampling is not guaranteed.

evidenceFields.description2: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor
evidenceFields.profile: Provides a research-project setting for sustainability questions supplied by organizations and companies in the Zeeland delta. Small teams work with an external advisor to review literature, formulate a research question, plan and execute an investigation, and develop a final product, design or report. The substantive topic and practical techniques depend on the partner project; the common focus is an evidence-based research process and engagement with external stakeholders.
evidenceFields.topics: Regionally situated sustainability problems; Research-question development; Research planning; Academic literature and evidence; External stakeholder collaboration; Applied sustainability investigation
evidenceFields.methods: Literature review; Research design

courses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courses.contribution: Direct empirical design, sampling, measurement, inference and regression in R support reliable investigation of environmental and social questions; the research project does not guarantee a marine topic.

evidenceFields.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.

courses.name: Conservation Biology
courses.contribution: Direct conservation reasoning about fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, climate pressure and species protection supports assessing threats and conservation responses in marine ecosystems.

evidenceFields.description2: This course explores environmental conservation through biological and social science perspectives. Topics include biodiversity importance, threats to ecosystems, conservation methods, and tools to monitor and protect nature. It also covers national and international laws, policies, and initiatives aimed at preserving ecosystems and ensuring a sustainable future for current and future generations.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces conservation biology through biodiversity loss, its human causes and possible responses. Students examine habitat destruction and fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change, disasters and extinction, followed by conservation planning, species management and conservation in altered landscapes. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.

courses.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
courses.contribution: Direct social-movement theory, environmental justice and Environmental Justice Atlas cases support analysing contested resource use, distributional harm and civic responses; marine policy specialization is not asserted.

evidenceFields.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

courses.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
courses.contribution: Direct population and community ecology, food webs, energy/matter fluxes and ecological modelling in R provide mechanisms for understanding marine ecosystems and conservation effects.

evidenceFields.description2: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.

courses.name: Sustainability Essentials I
courses.contribution: Complementary chemical equilibria, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, thermodynamics and simple dynamic models supply natural-science tools for analysing marine environmental pressures; this is not an economic or legal course.

evidenceFields.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
evidenceFields.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.

courses.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
courses.contribution: Complementary cell structure, metabolism, DNA/heredity, gene expression and biotechnology establish biological foundations for marine-organism and molecular study; no marine field content is asserted.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.

courses.name: Dynamic Earth
courses.contribution: Complementary sedimentation, geomorphology, geological history and Earth-system/climate interactions explain physical settings and land-to-sea processes relevant to coastal change; it is not advanced physical oceanography.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth, lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces Earth science by linking surface geology to deep-Earth and geophysical processes. evidenceFields.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.

courses.contribution: Direct marine ecology and physical/chemical oceanography connect production, microbial processes, estuaries, shores, reefs and deep/polar seas with fisheries, aquaculture, acidification and plastic pollution.

evidenceFields.description2: Studies ecological processes in marine environments such as estuaries, rocky shores and coral reefs. Examines human impacts and includes guest lectures, lab visits, excursions and field work, culminating in an essay.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines marine ecological processes, ocean systems and human impacts on the sea. Physical and chemical oceanography support the study of primary and secondary production, microbial ecology, and habitats from estuaries and shores to the open ocean, deep sea and polar regions. Student seminars address fisheries, aquaculture, acidification, sea-level rise and plastic pollution. A multimedia outreach project translates a marine biological topic for a public audience.

evidenceFields.description2: Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering, mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises geochemical modelling and a case study.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines chemical and biological controls on near-surface Earth systems, especially interactions among water, minerals, rocks and soils. Laboratory investigations and geochemical modelling connect these processes to contaminant behaviour, wastewater treatment, remediation and resource recovery. courses.name: Building with Nature

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. evidenceFields.profile: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.

courses.name: Law, Society & Justice
courses.contribution: Direct legal systems, public/private/international law, case-law analysis and legal argument support understanding institutional rules and rights relevant to ocean use; it does not provide a full maritime-law sequence.

evidenceFields.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.

courses.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
courses.contribution: Direct appraisal of food-production systems, biodiversity impacts and farming innovations, including aquaculture, supports the food/environment connection. The course is broadly agricultural and does not replace a specialist marine-food or aquaculture sequence.

evidenceFields.description2: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines how food production can balance human needs with environmental impacts. Students assess current agriculture, horticulture and animal husbandry, their effects on biodiversity and ecosystems, and alternative practices and innovations. Aquaculture, alternative animal-protein sources and farming for other industries extend the comparison. A literature-based project critically investigates a chosen sustainable-farming question and reports the evidence without prescribing a single preferred approach.

courses.name: Living with Water
courses.contribution: Direct Zeeland delta inquiry connects sea-level rise, salinisation, flood/freshwater management, law and ecological trade-offs; evaluating engineered and nature-based responses supports coastal adaptation appraisal.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines how delta societies manage water risks and opportunities, using Zeeland as a central case. Physical and ecological challenges such as flooding, salinization, freshwater scarcity, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, considering trade-offs and long-term consequences. Site-based inquiry and a project apply these concepts to context-sensitive adaptation in a delta region.

courses.name: Governance of Sustainability
courses.contribution: Direct institutions, common-pool resources, participation, stakeholder analysis and policy evaluation in food/water/energy/climate support environmental resource governance; the Zeeland case is not guaranteed ocean governance.

evidenceFields.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
evidenceFields.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.

evidenceFields.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

courses.name: Econometrics
courses.contribution: Direct regression estimators, causal/predictive inference, specification tests and an empirical paper provide tools for analysing economic relationships and evaluating resource policies, not a dedicated marine-economics course.

evidenceFields.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

courses.name: Mathematical Methods
courses.contribution: Direct calculus, differential equations, numerical integration and dynamic-model implementation provide mathematical tools for ecological and environmental modelling.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
evidenceFields.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
evidenceFields.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

courses.name: Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations
courses.contribution: Direct geoscience risk and adaptation tools, climate-driven hazards, droughts, mining disasters and toxic algal blooms support assessing environmental/coastal risk within the scope of its official description.

evidenceFields.description2: Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and toxic algae blooms.

courses.name: Biochemistry
courses.contribution: Complementary enzymes, biomolecular function, respiration and energy/lipid/nitrogen metabolism support the biological mechanisms underlying organismal growth and production. This is biochemistry, not aquatic-animal physiology or aquaculture management.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.
evidenceFields.topics: Water and weak bonds; Amino acids and protein structure; Protein-biochemistry techniques; Enzyme action, kinetics, regulation and inhibition; Hemoglobin; Carbohydrates and lipids; Metabolic organization; Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis; Citric-acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; Glycogen and pentose-phosphate metabolism; Fatty-acid and lipid metabolism; Nitrogen and urea cycle; Biochemical mechanisms of disease
evidenceFields.methods: Biochemical pathway and disease-mechanism analysis; Primary-literature review

courses.name: Climate Change
courses.contribution: Direct climate feedbacks, sea-level rise, ocean acidification and ecosystem impacts connect physical pressures with mitigation, adaptation, justice and stakeholder communication.

evidenceFields.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
evidenceFields.discipline: Climate science; Environmental studies; Climate governance
evidenceFields.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
evidenceFields.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

courses.name: Molecular Cell Biology
courses.contribution: Direct molecular cell structure, proteins, membranes, gene expression, signalling and energy processes support the cellular dimension of marine life. The literature project is biomedical, not a guaranteed marine investigation.

evidenceFields.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
evidenceFields.topics: Cellular components and bioenergetics; Proteins and membranes; Cytoskeleton; DNA replication and repair; Genomes; Regulation of gene expression; Membrane transport and trafficking; Cell-signalling pathways; Cell division and fate; Tissue organization; Stem cells; Cancer; Molecular mechanisms of drug action
evidenceFields.methods: Critical analysis of primary molecular-biology literature; Evaluation of research-method limitations and reproducibility; Thermodynamic free-energy calculations; Molecular mechanism analysis

courses.name: Soils & Aquifers
courses.contribution: Direct soils, shallow aquifers, salinisation, freshwater interventions, field sampling and geophysical surveys support understanding land-water and coastal-groundwater conditions, not open-ocean circulation.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores soils and aquifers through fieldwork and lab analyses. Covers soil formation, properties, health and remediation and investigates mapping aquifers for geothermal energy, coastal defence and freshwater resource assessment.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines soils and shallow aquifers through soil science, environmental chemistry and applied geophysics. Soil formation, functions, quality and threats connect to texture, structure, composition, biological activity and salinization. Field sampling and laboratory investigations characterize soil properties and sediment-cell behaviour. Seismic, electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveys investigate physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers. Students document procedures and observations, process field data in Excel, interpret results and develop evidence-based field and laboratory reports.
evidenceFields.discipline: Soil science; Hydrogeology; Applied geophysics; Environmental chemistry
evidenceFields.topics: Soil formation, functions and taxonomy; Soil quality, amendments and threats; Soil texture, structure and aggregate stability; Soil moisture and organic matter; Soil chemistry, pH and metals; Soil biology; Sediment-cell behaviour; Shallow aquifers, salinization and freshwater interventions; Physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers; Seismology; Electrical resistivity; Electromagnetic surveying
evidenceFields.methods: Soil coring and field sampling; Visual soil-structure assessment (grass-VESS); Aggregate-stability, texture and sieve tests; Soil pH, moisture, organic-content and leaching analyses; Microscopy and SEM-EDS; Sample preparation for ICP/IC and interpretation of ICP results; Methylene-blue testing with spectrophotometry/titration; Seismic surveying; Electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveying; Field-data processing in Excel

courses.name: The Science of Evolution
courses.contribution: Direct natural selection, population genetics, adaptation, speciation and phylogeny support explaining marine biodiversity and evolutionary responses; this is evolutionary training across organisms, not aquatic life-history specialization.

evidenceFields.description2: Evolution is the unifying theory in biology. As such, an understanding of evolutionary biology is vital for understanding the natural world. In this course, we will discuss key concepts in evolution such as population genetics, variation and selection, speciation, macro-evolution and the origins of life. The importance of evolutionary concepts to all other fields of biology will be emphasized, as well as important implications of evolutionary processes in fields like human health and climate change.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines evolutionary theory from genetic mechanisms to the diversification and history of life. Students study natural selection, variation and drift, population and quantitative genetics, adaptation and sexual reproduction, then species concepts, speciation, phylogeny and macroevolution. Genomics, development, biogeography and coevolution extend the account across scales. A project reconstructs a chosen species' evolutionary history using Tinbergen's four questions.
evidenceFields.topics: Evidence for evolution; Molecular and Mendelian genetics; Natural selection and genetic drift; Multilocus and quantitative genetics; Adaptation and units of selection; Sexual reproduction; Species concepts and speciation; Phylogeny and classification; Evolutionary biogeography; Evolutionary genomics and development; Coevolution; Evolutionary rates, extinction and radiation
evidenceFields.methods: Evolutionary-history analysis using Tinbergen's four questions; Phylogenetic reconstruction

courses.name: Probability & Statistics
courses.contribution: Direct probability distributions, estimation, hypothesis tests, Bayesian reasoning and Monte Carlo methods support rigorous quantitative ecological research; this is mathematical statistics rather than a marine-methods field course.

evidenceFields.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
evidenceFields.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
evidenceFields.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
evidenceFields.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

courses.name: Earth System Science Tools
courses.contribution: Direct Earth-system interactions, system modelling, proxies and isotope tracers support climate reconstruction and environmental-flow reasoning within the official description; no detailed marine-current model is claimed.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.

courses.name: Public Economics
courses.contribution: Direct market failure, public goods, externalities, collective choice and efficiency/equity analysis support evaluating public intervention and competing uses of marine resources; applications are broader than the marine domain.

evidenceFields.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
evidenceFields.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
evidenceFields.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research

courses.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
courses.contribution: Complementary solar-panel/e-waste recycling, metal recovery and soil remediation provide chemical/laboratory tools for appraising resource and pollution consequences of sustainability interventions; this is not marine remediation or offshore design.

evidenceFields.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
evidenceFields.discipline: Environmental chemistry; Materials recycling; Environmental biotechnology
evidenceFields.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
evidenceFields.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations

courses.name: Machine Learning
courses.contribution: Direct regression/classification, model validation, prediction and unsupervised learning support the data-science part of analysing environmental systems; this does not reproduce coupled physical/social marine simulation.

evidenceFields.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
evidenceFields.discipline: Machine learning; Statistical learning; Data science
evidenceFields.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
evidenceFields.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

courses.name: Renewable System Design
courses.contribution: Direct technical/economic appraisal of energy use and solar, wind and bioenergy alternatives supports sustainable-energy decisions. Its company project does not guarantee offshore wind, marine engineering or a coastal topic.

evidenceFields.description2: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

targetSubstance: The closest response materially addresses the target’s defining marine ecological and human-environmental substance: marine biology/oceanography, ecosystem/biodiversity mechanisms, coastal nature-based interventions, water chemistry, GIS/data, food-production impacts and environmental economic/legal/governance analysis. Its coherence alone is not the comparability test. These actual contributions make it a meaningful response to integrated marine socio-ecological problems, while dedicated aquaculture, marine organismal/field methods, advanced ocean processes and a required marine thesis remain substantial limits. The biological route shifts weight to evolution, cell biology, biochemistry, laboratory work and statistics; the third shifts to physical coastal climate, spatial/data and energy/resource appraisal. None claims a specialist marine degree or offshore engineering.

alignmentFinding: Every exact UCR identity has one row and block. External placements were recomputed from actual content: ecology to Ecosystems, ocean chemistry to Environmental Biogeochemistry, NBS design to Building with Nature, coastal appraisal to Living with Water, statistics to Methods & Statistics, human research to Qualitative Research, law to Law/Society/Justice, resource-policy economics to Public Economics. Machine Learning addresses specifically statistical classification/fitting within the WUR modelling course, not coupled marine simulation. Generic sustainability introduction and partner-defined research are not matched to marine introduction or fieldwork. General Biodiversity is not matched to the specialist Marine Life component after the source-first challenge. Farming and flows correspondences are partial and explicitly bounded. Optional independent research is parallel to the 12-credit thesis and outside 24/180.

repairAndDependencies: Seven original prerequisite/offering conflicts resolved through valid course choices and schedules. No old offering restored, no cohort shifted and no missing planning horizon interpreted as a no-match.

Replaced broad-route Human Physiology, Infection & Immunity, Peace & Conflict and EU Politics with Ecosystems, Building with Nature, introductory law and qualitative inquiry. This strengthens actual marine/ecological, nature-based and resource-governance functions instead of attaching generic marine rationales to biomedical/security content.

Biological route replaces Human Physiology and Infection & Immunity with Biochemistry and Building with Nature. Molecular/biochemical and lab study is a bounded complement to marine organisms, not aquatic physiology training. Coastal route replaces Earth’s Resources with Marine Biology, strengthening the actual marine setting.

ENSSUST313 is only planned in the first term and has no formal prerequisite. It remains early applied sustainability research with partner-dependent scope, not a late capstone or guaranteed marine field investigation. Relevant foundations otherwise precede advanced applications where feasible. No new hard progression rule invented.

Description-only ENSENVI112, ENSENVI213, ENSSUST311, BENECON312 and GOSSOCI215 receive full consideration within their official descriptions. Selected course evidence and historical shared description reviews are preserved; no enrichment regeneration or source-class interface labels.

All affected concepts, labels, course rationales, schedules, qualitative/numerical distinctness, stopping decision, external placements, interest attribution and audience selections reassessed. The 180-credit comparator allocation is preserved while choice, safety, thesis preparation and portfolio rules are clarified.
